Speculative Decoding

Guess several tokens cheaply; let the target model decide which guesses survive.

§How to use this document

This is a companion to LLM Inference Systems and LLM Quantization. It assumes you know prefill, autoregressive decode, attention, and the KV cache. Read §0–§2 for the mechanism and its mathematics; §3 for the field’s chronological shifts; §4 and §4+ for landmark papers, their variants and the 2026 frontier; §5–§8 for correctness, engineering, and evidence. The guide combines 26 original paper figures/table crops with explanatory redrawings. Each paper figure has a source link, an archived local PDF, and a link to its full-resolution crop. The surrounding text explains the mechanism and the figure’s evidential limits; the bibliography also covers important variants without implying that every cited paper is a new landmark.

The thesis, up front

Speculation saves serial target-model steps, not necessarily total arithmetic. A draft is valuable when it is cheap and frequently agrees with the target. The verifier must be efficient enough to check several candidate positions at once. The choice of acceptance rule determines whether the result is exactly the target distribution or only an empirically similar output. [1]

0The central idea

Autoregressive decoding has a serial dependency: token t+1t+1t+1 depends on token ttt. Speculative decoding moves some of that serial work to a cheap proposer and checks many proposed positions in one target pass.

Let ppp be the target model’s next-token distribution and qqq a cheaper draft distribution. Starting from a confirmed prefix, the drafter proposes KKK tokens in order. The target runs on the entire proposed continuation under a causal mask and returns distributions for positions 1…K+11\ldots K+11…K+1. Each position’s logits are conditional on the proposed prefix before it. We consume only the longest valid prefix of the draft, then one target-derived correction or bonus token. An unaccepted suffix is discarded. This is one target invocation but generally more target computation than a one-token invocation. [1] [2]

The reason a target pass can check several positions is ordinary teacher forcing: with all candidate tokens supplied, a causal Transformer computes their conditional logits in parallel. The target weights can be reused across positions, which helps most when a single-token decode is limited by memory traffic. At high batch size, long context, or wide trees, verification may become compute or KV-bandwidth limited and the benefit can shrink. [1] [15]

1Exact verification

“The target checks it” is incomplete. A precise acceptance and correction rule makes the algorithm correct.

1.1 Greedy verification

For deterministic greedy decoding, the target’s answer at a position is arg⁡max⁡pi\arg\max p_iargmaxpi​. Compare that answer with draft token did_{i}di​ along the drafted context. Commit the longest matching prefix. At the first mismatch, emit the target’s arg⁡max⁡pi\arg\max p_iargmaxpi​. If all KKK draft tokens match, emit the target’s token from pk+1p_{k+1}pk+1​ as a bonus. Thus a round emits between 1 and K+1K+1K+1 tokens. The result is the same greedy token sequence as the target, assuming the same target weights, prompt, decoding constraints, and numerics. [1]

draft:       the | quick | brown | fox
target argmax:the | quick | black | ...
commit:      the | quick | black        (the draft's “fox” is invalid)

1.2 Exact speculative sampling

For random sampling, comparing the draft token with the target’s sampled token would reject too often. Leviathan et al. and Chen et al. use a coupled rejection rule. At draft position iii, the draft samples di∼qid_{i} \sim q_{i}di​∼qi​; the target computes pip_{i}pi​ under the same drafted history. Accept did_{i}di​ with probability min⁡ ⁣(1,pi(di)qi(di))\min\!\left(1,\frac{p_i(d_i)}{q_i(d_i)}\right)min(1,qi​(di​)pi​(di​)​). At the first rejection, sample a replacement from the normalized positive residual (pi−qi)+(p_{i} - q_{i})_{+}(pi​−qi​)+​ and stop the round. If all KKK drafts survive, draw one bonus token from pk+1p_{k+1}pk+1​. [1] [2]

ai(di)=min⁡ ⁣(1,pi(di)qi(di))ri(x)=[pi(x)−qi(x)]+∑y[pi(y)−qi(y)]+All drafts accepted:xbonus∼pK+1\begin{aligned}a_i(d_i)&=\min\!\left(1,\frac{p_i(d_i)}{q_i(d_i)}\right)\\ r_i(x)&=\frac{[p_i(x)-q_i(x)]_+}{\sum_y[p_i(y)-q_i(y)]_+}\\ \text{All drafts accepted:}\quad x_{\mathrm{bonus}}&\sim p_{K+1}\end{aligned}ai​(di​)ri​(x)All drafts accepted:xbonus​​=min(1,qi​(di​)pi​(di​)​)=∑y​[pi​(y)−qi​(y)]+​[pi​(x)−qi​(x)]+​​∼pK+1​​

Here pip_{i}pi​ and qiq_{i}qi​ mean the actual sampling distributions after temperature, top-k/top-p, masks, penalties, or other logit processing, rather than unadjusted logits. The draft may have a very different distribution; the acceptance rate changes, but the rule still samples from ppp if implemented consistently. If the rejection probability is zero, the residual is never needed. If q(d)=0q(d)=0q(d)=0, that token cannot be proposed by qqq. [1]

1.3 Full proof: acceptance plus correction preserves the target law

The theorem. Fix a confirmed history h and a finite token vocabulary V. Let p(x|h) be the target distribution we want and q(x|h) the actual proposal distribution. Sample D ∼ q and independently U ∼ Uniform(0,1). Accept D if U ≤ min(1,p(D)/q(D)); otherwise emit a fresh token from r(x) ∝ [p(x)−q(x)]+, where [z]+ = max(z,0). The final emitted token X has law p. The draft need not be accurate or share target parameters. The following expands the exact-sampling argument of Leviathan et al. and Chen et al. into its probability-accounting steps.

Step 1: compute accepted probability mass, not only conditional acceptance

For a token x with q(x)>0, acceptance conditional on proposing x is a(x)=min(1,p(x)/q(x)). But the probability of emitting x via the accepted branch includes the probability that x was proposed:

Pr⁡(X=x,accept∣h)=Pr⁡(D=x∣h)Pr⁡(accept∣D=x,h)=q(x)min⁡ ⁣(1,p(x)q(x))=min⁡(p(x),q(x))(1)\begin{aligned}\Pr(X=x,\mathrm{accept}\mid h)&=\Pr(D=x\mid h)\Pr(\mathrm{accept}\mid D=x,h)\\ &=q(x)\min\!\left(1,\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right)\\ &=\min(p(x),q(x))\qquad(1)\end{aligned}Pr(X=x,accept∣h)​=Pr(D=x∣h)Pr(accept∣D=x,h)=q(x)min(1,q(x)p(x)​)=min(p(x),q(x))(1)​

If q(x)=0, this contribution is zero without ever dividing by zero. Define the total accepted mass α=Σxmin(p(x),q(x)). The accepted branch delivers the overlap of the two distributions; it has not yet delivered the target's entire mass.

Step 2: prove that the missing mass equals the rejection probability

Both distributions sum to one. Thus the surplus of q over p equals its deficit elsewhere. Writing the positive and negative parts explicitly gives:

∑x(q(x)−p(x))=0∑x[q(x)−p(x)]+=∑x[p(x)−q(x)]+Pr⁡(reject∣h)=1−α=∑x{q(x)−min⁡(p(x),q(x))}=∑x[q(x)−p(x)]+=∑x[p(x)−q(x)]+≡Z(2)\begin{aligned}\sum_x(q(x)-p(x))&=0\\ \sum_x[q(x)-p(x)]_+&=\sum_x[p(x)-q(x)]_+\\ \Pr(\mathrm{reject}\mid h)&=1-\alpha\\ &=\sum_x\{q(x)-\min(p(x),q(x))\}\\ &=\sum_x[q(x)-p(x)]_+\\ &=\sum_x[p(x)-q(x)]_+\equiv Z\qquad(2)\end{aligned}x∑​(q(x)−p(x))x∑​[q(x)−p(x)]+​Pr(reject∣h)​=0=x∑​[p(x)−q(x)]+​=1−α=x∑​{q(x)−min(p(x),q(x))}=x∑​[q(x)−p(x)]+​=x∑​[p(x)−q(x)]+​≡Z(2)​

The correction distribution is r(x)=[p(x)−q(x)]+/Z when Z>0. If Z=0, p=q and every proposal is accepted; no residual sample is required. Unlike ordinary rejection sampling with a global envelope, this algorithm still emits a token after a rejection by correcting the missing mass.

Step 3: combine the two mutually exclusive branches

Pr⁡(X=x∣h)=Pr⁡(X=x,accept∣h)+Pr⁡(X=x,reject∣h)=min⁡(p(x),q(x))+Pr⁡(reject∣h)r(x)=min⁡(p(x),q(x))+Z[p(x)−q(x)]+Z=min⁡(p(x),q(x))+[p(x)−q(x)]+=p(x)(3)\begin{aligned}\Pr(X=x\mid h)&=\Pr(X=x,\mathrm{accept}\mid h)\\ &\quad+\Pr(X=x,\mathrm{reject}\mid h)\\ &=\min(p(x),q(x))+\Pr(\mathrm{reject}\mid h)r(x)\\ &=\min(p(x),q(x))+Z\frac{[p(x)-q(x)]_+}{Z}\\ &=\min(p(x),q(x))+[p(x)-q(x)]_+\\ &=p(x)\qquad(3)\end{aligned}Pr(X=x∣h)​=Pr(X=x,accept∣h)+Pr(X=x,reject∣h)=min(p(x),q(x))+Pr(reject∣h)r(x)=min(p(x),q(x))+ZZ[p(x)−q(x)]+​​=min(p(x),q(x))+[p(x)−q(x)]+​=p(x)(3)​

The last equality follows by two cases. If p(x)≤q(x), acceptance already supplies p(x) and the residual supplies zero. If p(x)>q(x), acceptance supplies q(x) and the residual supplies p(x)−q(x). This is why arbitrarily poor drafts affect speed but not the mathematical target distribution.

Step 4: extend from one token to the entire generated sequence

A one-token marginal identity alone is insufficient: two algorithms can have the same marginal at every position but different dependencies. We need the identity conditional on every confirmed prefix. Imagine a logically sequential implementation that samples one proposal, applies the above correction, and repeats at the new prefix. For every reachable h, its next-token kernel equals p(·|h), so the chain rule gives:

Pspec(X1:n=x1:n∣prompt)=∏i=1nPspec(Xi=xi∣prompt,x1:i−1)=∏i=1np(xi∣prompt,x1:i−1)=Ptarget(x1:n∣prompt)(4)\begin{aligned}P_{\mathrm{spec}}(X_{1:n}=x_{1:n}\mid\mathrm{prompt})&=\prod_{i=1}^nP_{\mathrm{spec}}(X_i=x_i\mid\mathrm{prompt},x_{1:i-1})\\ &=\prod_{i=1}^np(x_i\mid\mathrm{prompt},x_{1:i-1})\\ &=P_{\mathrm{target}}(x_{1:n}\mid\mathrm{prompt})\qquad(4)\end{aligned}Pspec​(X1:n​=x1:n​∣prompt)​=i=1∏n​Pspec​(Xi​=xi​∣prompt,x1:i−1​)=i=1∏n​p(xi​∣prompt,x1:i−1​)=Ptarget​(x1:n​∣prompt)(4)​

Why batching does not change this sequential experiment: drafting an autoregressive chain early merely precomputes q-conditioned proposals. Verifying the whole chain early computes each target distribution under that same candidate prefix. Before the first rejection, candidate prefixes equal confirmed prefixes. At the rejection, all later predictions use a now-invalid history and must be discarded. A fresh round starts from the corrected history. If all proposals survive, the bonus token is a direct draw from p at the confirmed extended prefix. Thus the batched execution is a rescheduling of valid sequential kernels; it cannot commit target evaluations from an unconfirmed branch. Treating EOS as a token and applying the same stopping rule preserves the distribution of complete terminated sequences as well.

The scope of the theorem

This proof covers the chain algorithm with its actual proposal law and independent acceptance randomness. A tree, confidence-selected candidate, diffusion block or cached branch needs an acceptance rule consistent with that proposal process. In particular, selecting a candidate after seeing its token or confidence can change q. Using the pre-selection q in a ratio is not automatically valid. Greedy exactness can be proved instead by induction on matching argmax tokens. Neither theorem says that a relaxed probability threshold preserves an arbitrary sampling distribution.

Temperature, top-p/top-k, grammar masks and penalties define the processed distributions p and q used in the theorem. The reference and verifier must use the same processed target, positions and causal state. Floating-point kernel differences are a separate implementation question. Distributional equality does not imply identical text from two runs with the same RNG seed, because the samplers consume randomness differently.

Proof exercise 1: why is sampling directly from p on rejection wrong?

It produces min(p(x),q(x))+(1−α)p(x). For p=(0.2,0.5,0.3), q=(0.5,0.4,0.1), α=0.7, so the result is (0.26,0.55,0.19), not p. Acceptance has already emitted a biased subset; replacement must fill the complementary mass.

Proof exercise 2: must the draft cover the target's support?

No. Let p=(0.4,0.6) and q=(1,0). Only the first token is proposed; it is accepted with probability 0.4. All rejection mass 0.6 goes to the second token through r=(0,1). Thus target tokens absent from the draft support are still generated correctly. A residual implementation that only enumerates the draft's support would fail.

Proof exercise 3: derive acceptance from total variation

For each x, min(p,q)=(p+q−|p−q|)/2. Summing yields α=1−½Σ|p−q|=1−TV(p,q). Therefore distribution alignment is the right objective for acceptance; matching only argmax predictions does not determine α.

1.4 The coupling interpretation: why this acceptance is optimal for one proposal

Let X∼qX\sim qX∼q be the proposed token and Y∼pY\sim pY∼p the token eventually emitted at a fixed confirmed prefix. Any joint distribution with these marginals satisfies P(X=Y=x)≤min⁡(q(x),p(x))P(X=Y=x) \le \min(q(x),p(x))P(X=Y=x)≤min(q(x),p(x)). Summing over tokens bounds the probability of reusing the proposal by ∑xmin⁡(p(x),q(x))\sum_x\min(p(x),q(x))∑x​min(p(x),q(x)). The acceptance–residual construction attains that bound: it is a maximal coupling of the two distributions. Independent sampling and checking equality achieves only ∑xp(x)q(x)\sum_xp(x)q(x)∑x​p(x)q(x). Even when p=qp=qp=q, independent draws frequently disagree, while maximal coupling accepts every proposal. The saving comes from choosing the dependence between samples correctly, without changing either required marginal. [1]

A common incorrect implementation accepts with the usual ratio but, on rejection, samples directly from ppp. Write α=∑xmin⁡(p(x),q(x))\alpha=\sum_x\min(p(x),q(x))α=∑x​min(p(x),q(x)). Its output mass becomes min⁡(p(x),q(x))+(1−α)p(x)\min(p(x),q(x))+(1-\alpha )p(x)min(p(x),q(x))+(1−α)p(x), generally different from p(x)p(x)p(x). Rejection has already revealed information about the proposal: the correction must fill precisely the probability mass that acceptance did not deliver. This is why a verifier needs the complete residual distribution at the rejected position, rather than just the target probability of the proposed token.

A deterministic proposal still has a proposal law

If a lookup rule always proposes token ddd for a particular prefix, its law is q(x)=1[x=d]q(x)=1[x=d]q(x)=1[x=d]. An exact stochastic verifier accepts it with probability p(d)p(d)p(d); on rejection it samples ppp conditioned on x≠dx\ne dx=d. There is no need to invent a neural draft score. For a retrieved tree or a sequence selected from random alternatives, however, the law is more complicated: identifying the actual proposal/selection process is part of the correctness proof. Greedy longest-prefix verification avoids this stochastic-law problem because its target is a deterministic sequence.

This viewpoint also separates model approximation from sampler approximation. A heavily quantized or sparse-context draft can be arbitrarily inaccurate and still be corrected exactly. Changing target logits, truncating the residual to an approximate vocabulary, or applying inconsistent output constraints changes the distribution being preserved. In implementation, define the processed target distribution once and use that same definition for the serial reference, acceptance, residual, and bonus sampling.

Derivation: from a one-token correction to the whole sequence law

The one-step mass identity above is necessary, but an implementation must also preserve the history on which each distribution is conditioned. Let h be the confirmed token sequence, pₕ the target's actual processed sampling distribution, and qₕ the proposal distribution. Fix the ordinary sequential algorithm: draft each next candidate from q conditioned on its ancestors, use independent acceptance uniforms, stop at the first rejection, and discard all descendants of a rejected candidate.

For a candidate x, the joint probability of proposing and accepting x is min(pₕ(x),qₕ(x)). Write Rₕ=Σx(pₕ(x)−qₕ(x))₊. Since both distributions sum to one, the excess proposal mass and missing target mass are equal:

∑x[qh(x)−ph(x)]+=∑x[ph(x)−qh(x)]+=RhPr⁡(next token=x∣h)=min⁡(ph(x),qh(x))+Rh[ph(x)−qh(x)]+Rh=ph(x)\begin{aligned}\sum_x[q_h(x)-p_h(x)]_+&=\sum_x[p_h(x)-q_h(x)]_+=R_h\\ \Pr(\text{next token}=x\mid h)&=\min(p_h(x),q_h(x))\\ &\quad+R_h\frac{[p_h(x)-q_h(x)]_+}{R_h}\\ &=p_h(x)\end{aligned}x∑​[qh​(x)−ph​(x)]+​Pr(next token=x∣h)​=x∑​[ph​(x)−qh​(x)]+​=Rh​=min(ph​(x),qh​(x))+Rh​Rh​[ph​(x)−qh​(x)]+​​=ph​(x)​

When Rₕ=0, rejection never occurs and no division is performed. If x has qₕ(x)=0 but pₕ(x)>0, x cannot appear as a proposal but receives its correct mass through the residual. Absolute continuity of p with respect to q is therefore unnecessary for this correction.

Now induct over committed positions. Suppose the probability of a committed prefix x₁:t is the target product. Accepted candidates have target states computed on that same prefix; at a rejection, descendants are discarded and the replacement defines the next prefix. A bonus token is sampled directly from the target. In the standard algorithm, later draft randomness conditioned on its ancestor tokens is not reweighted by earlier independent acceptance uniforms. Thus the next conditional kernel remains the one above, and the chain rule gives:

Pspec(x1:t+1)=Pspec(x1:t)p(xt+1∣x1:t)=∏i=1t+1p(xi∣x1:i−1)\begin{aligned}P_{\mathrm{spec}}(x_{1:t+1})&=P_{\mathrm{spec}}(x_{1:t})p(x_{t+1}\mid x_{1:t})\\ &=\prod_{i=1}^{t+1}p(x_i\mid x_{1:i-1})\end{aligned}Pspec​(x1:t+1​)​=Pspec​(x1:t​)p(xt+1​∣x1:t​)=i=1∏t+1​p(xi​∣x1:i−1​)​

This proof also identifies concrete failure modes. Logits after a rejected token are conditioned on a different history. Sampling a selected best-of-many candidate while correcting against the unselected q uses a different proposal law. Applying a constraint mask to the emitted token but not to p in the correction changes the kernel. An adaptive policy that filters candidates based on their identities needs its actual conditional proposal distribution or a separate correctness proof.

At the level of real arithmetic, equal kernels imply equal sequence distributions. Different floating-point kernels can slightly change p; that is a separate numerical question. Equality of distributions does not require equal random-number consumption or identical text from the same seed.

Exercise — Recover a token the drafter never proposes

Let p=(0.2,0.3,0.5) and q=(0.6,0.4,0) over A,B,C. Compute accepted probability mass, rejection probability, the residual distribution, and the final output law.

Show worked solution

Accepted mass is min(p,q)=(0.2,0.3,0), summing to 0.5. Conditional acceptance probabilities are 1/3 for an A proposal and 3/4 for a B proposal; C is never proposed. Missing mass is (p−q)₊=(0,0,0.5), so rejection probability is 0.5 and its normalized residual always emits C. Adding accepted and corrected mass gives (0.2,0.3,0.5)=p. This example shows why truncating a drafter's vocabulary need not destroy exactness, provided the target residual remains available.

2The speed equation

More accepted tokens per target pass only help if the extra draft and verification work costs less than the target steps saved.

2.1 Acceptance, depth, and verification cost

Let AiA_{i}Ai​ be the event that the first iii draft tokens are all accepted. The exact expected number of emitted tokens per round, away from end-of-sequence and output caps, is 1+∑i=1KPr⁡(Ai)1+\sum_{i=1}^K\Pr(A_i)1+∑i=1K​Pr(Ai​). If each conditional acceptance is approximately a constant α\alpha α, this becomes a capped geometric sum. The maximum is K+1K+1K+1; even a perfect draft cannot exceed it. [1]

E=1+∑i=1KPr⁡(Ai)Econstant-α≈1+α+α2+⋯+αK=1−αK+11−α(α≠1)S≈Ttarget(1)EKTdraft(1)+Tverify(K)+Tmisc\begin{aligned}E&=1+\sum_{i=1}^K\Pr(A_i)\\ E_{\mathrm{constant}\text{-}\alpha}&\approx1+\alpha+\alpha^2+\cdots+\alpha^K\\ &=\frac{1-\alpha^{K+1}}{1-\alpha}\quad(\alpha\ne1)\\ S&\approx\frac{T_{\mathrm{target}}(1)E}{KT_{\mathrm{draft}}(1)+T_{\mathrm{verify}}(K)+T_{\mathrm{misc}}}\end{aligned}EEconstant-α​S​=1+i=1∑K​Pr(Ai​)≈1+α+α2+⋯+αK=1−α1−αK+1​(α=1)≈KTdraft​(1)+Tverify​(K)+Tmisc​Ttarget​(1)E​​

Tverify(K)T_{\mathrm{verify}}(K)Tverify​(K) is the wall time for one target invocation that scores the KKK drafted positions plus the bonus distribution; it is not automatically equal to Ttarget(1)T_{\mathrm{target}}(1)Ttarget​(1). Leviathan et al.’s compact formula E1+Kc\frac E{1+Kc}1+KcE​ assumes verification takes about one baseline target step and a draft step costs fraction ccc of that step. Those assumptions are useful for intuition and must be checked on actual hardware. [1]

For example, if K=4K=4K=4 and α=0.7\alpha =0.7α=0.7, E≈2.77E\approx 2.77E≈2.77. If each draft token costs 0.050.050.05 baseline target steps and verification costs 1.21.21.2 such steps, the rough speedup is 2.774⋅0.05+1.2≈1.98×\frac{2.77}{4\cdot0.05+1.2}\approx1.98\times4⋅0.05+1.22.77​≈1.98×. A wider draft improves EEE with diminishing returns while its cost and the verifier’s workload keep growing.

Derivation: accepted length without the constant-acceptance shortcut

Fix K proposed positions, assume no EOS or output cap inside the round, and assume the verifier emits one correction token at the first failure or one bonus token after full acceptance. Let A be the number of accepted draft tokens and L=A+1 the number of committed tokens. For any integer A between zero and K, A=Σi=1ᴷ1[A≥i]. Taking expectations proves the tail-sum identity.

Si=Pr⁡(first i proposals accepted),S0=1E[L]=1+∑i=1KSiai=Pr⁡(position i accepted∣first i−1 accepted)Si=∏j=1iajE[L]=1+∑i=1K∏j=1iaj\begin{aligned}S_i&=\Pr(\text{first }i\text{ proposals accepted}),\quad S_0=1\\ \mathbb E[L]&=1+\sum_{i=1}^KS_i\\ a_i&=\Pr(\text{position }i\text{ accepted}\mid\text{first }i-1\text{ accepted})\\ S_i&=\prod_{j=1}^ia_j\\ \mathbb E[L]&=1+\sum_{i=1}^K\prod_{j=1}^ia_j\end{aligned}Si​E[L]ai​Si​E[L]​=Pr(first i proposals accepted),S0​=1=1+i=1∑K​Si​=Pr(position i accepted∣first i−1 accepted)=j=1∏i​aj​=1+i=1∑K​j=1∏i​aj​​

This product uses the probability chain rule, not independence. Each aᵢ averages over the histories that actually survive to i. It generally differs from the unconditional acceptance rate at that position on all drafted paths. Replacing every aᵢ by α yields the familiar geometric sum (1−αᴷ⁺¹)/(1−α), with limit K+1 at α=1. That is a workload model, not an identity for arbitrary language-model trajectories.

An EOS or maximum output length can remove the bonus and shorten the committed block. The always-valid formula is E[L]=Σℓ≥1 P(L≥ℓ) using the actual termination policy. Counting an un-emitted bonus exaggerates speedups on short outputs.

If repeated rounds have costs Cᵣ and rewards Lᵣ, measured throughput is ΣᵣLᵣ/ΣᵣCᵣ. Under stationary ergodic rounds with finite means, its long-run limit is E[L]/E[C]; an independent regenerative-cycle model is one sufficient special case. It is generally not E[L/C]. Language-model rounds change with context and load, so report the observed totals or a clearly specified workload average instead of assuming stationarity silently.

Exercise — Different acceptance at different depths

K=3, and the acceptance probabilities conditional on reaching each position are 0.9, 0.5 and 0.2. Find E[L]. Separately, two equally common cycle types have (L,C)=(2,1 ms) and (4,4 ms). Find aggregate tokens/ms and the mean of per-cycle rates.

Show worked solution

Survival probabilities are S₁=0.9, S₂=0.45, S₃=0.09, giving E[L]=1+0.9+0.45+0.09=2.44. Multiplying unconditional marginal acceptance rates would not be justified unless they equal these conditional rates. For the two cycle types, aggregate throughput is (2+4)/(1+4)=1.2 tokens/ms. Averaging individual rates gives (2/1+4/4)/2=1.5 tokens/ms, which overweights the shorter cycle.

2.2 Interactive estimator

Estimate one-path speedup

A teaching model with independent equal acceptance probabilities. All costs are in units of one baseline target decode step.

Bars show the probability that the first i draft tokens survive. This estimate ignores EOS, changing acceptance across positions, scheduling, and cache costs.

Derivation: when is one more draft position worth its cost?

Let Gₖ=E[Lₖ] and Cₖ>0 be expected round latency for a fixed candidate depth K under a fixed workload model. Suppose extending to K+1 leaves the first K proposal laws unchanged, so Gₖ₊₁−Gₖ=Sₖ₊₁. Write ΔC=Cₖ₊₁−Cₖ>0. Compare the two throughput ratios by cross-multiplication:

GK+SK+1CK+ΔC>GKCK⟺CKSK+1>GKΔC⟺SK+1ΔC>GKCK\begin{aligned}\frac{G_K+S_{K+1}}{C_K+\Delta C}&>\frac{G_K}{C_K}\\ \Longleftrightarrow\quad C_KS_{K+1}&>G_K\Delta C\\ \Longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{S_{K+1}}{\Delta C}&>\frac{G_K}{C_K}\end{aligned}CK​+ΔCGK​+SK+1​​⟺CK​SK+1​⟺ΔCSK+1​​​>CK​GK​​>GK​ΔC>CK​GK​​​

The extra position must have better marginal committed tokens per millisecond than the current average. With a constant per-position acceptance α, Sₖ₊₁=αᴷ⁺¹ decays exponentially; if incremental cost stays positive, sufficiently deep drafting becomes unattractive even when α is high. A faster or more accurate drafter changes both sides of the comparison.

The calculation is local. It gives a globally optimal stopping point only under additional structure, such as diminishing marginal gain/cost ratios. Kernel tile boundaries, tree changes, shared launch overhead and load-dependent batching can make cost non-smooth or even temporarily flat; then enumerate feasible depths using a measured cost model. A latency SLO or memory limit can exclude the throughput maximizer.

For an adaptive policy, condition both expected gain and cost on information available when making the decision. Stopping before sampling the next candidate based on the existing prefix is different from seeing many candidates, selecting a favorable one and pretending its proposal law is unchanged. The first can preserve the ordinary proposal kernel; the second needs the selection probability in the proof. This scheduling argument never permits accepting a token merely because it is high confidence.

Exercise — A latency model selects the draft depth

Assume α=0.8, target verification costs 4 ms independent of depth in this toy regime, and drafting costs K ms. Thus Cₖ=4+K ms and Gₖ=Σi=0ᴷ0.8ⁱ. Compare K=0,1,2,3,4.

Among these choices, K=3 is best. From K=3 to K=4, the marginal gain/cost is 0.8⁴/1=0.4096 tokens/ms, below the current 2.952/7≈0.4217. Because gains keep shrinking and cost increments remain one, deeper choices also lose in this particular model. Real verification latency need not remain flat.

3How the field developed

The history is a sequence of bottlenecks. First remove serial target calls; then make the draft cheaper and better aligned; then spend verification on better candidate structures; finally co-design the drafter with training and the serving runtime.

3.1 Landmark papers and their descendant lines

Stage 1: correctness. Blockwise decoding made the longest verified prefix the unit of progress. The 2023 exact-sampling papers added a residual correction that preserves the target’s full stochastic distribution. Stage 2: proposal quality. Small-model distillation and target-attached heads increased acceptance without paying for a second large model. Stage 3: proposal geometry. Token trees represented alternatives, and dynamic tree algorithms chose which branches deserved scarce verification slots. Stage 4: systems. Parallel drafting, KV-aware drafters, and overlapped execution targeted wall time under real serving loads. These stages overlap in publication date and a new method may combine ideas from several. [1] [7] [16] [20]

3.2 Four independent design axes

A list of method names obscures the design. Place any system on four axes: draft source (small LM, target heads/features/layers, stored text, or parallel target iterations); candidate geometry (one chain, a tree, a graph, or a block); verification fidelity (same greedy text, same sampling distribution, or approximate quality); and runtime (single GPU, offloaded, distributed, or high-concurrency). This is a teaching synthesis of the generation/verification taxonomies in the 2024 and 2025 surveys. [16] [20]

LineageLandmarkKey variants introduced laterMain bottleneck attacked
Dual-model exact samplingLeviathan / ChenDistillSpec, Online SD, SpecDec++, OuroborosAcceptance and serial draft work
Multi-path verificationSpecInferStaged SD, Sequoia, OPT-Tree, DySpec, SpecExecWasted verification on a single failed chain
Target-attached predictionsMedusaHydra, ReDrafter, Speculative Streaming, MTPSeparate draft weights and poor multi-step guesses
Feature-conditioned draftEAGLEEAGLE-2, HASS, EAGLE-3, FalconDraft–target representation mismatch
Self / training-free draftDraft & Verify; prompt lookupLayerSkip, Kangaroo, SWIFT; REST, Token Recycling, SuffixDecodingDraft memory and training burden

Diffusion / parallel blocksSpecDiffDiffuSpec, SpecDiff-2, TiDAR, DFlash, DARTreeSerial proposal passes and block coherence

A path proposes one sequence; a tree offers alternatives at different depths; a block predicts several positions in parallel. A tree can rescue a round after one poor proposal but costs target positions. The same proposal source can be paired with different geometries or acceptance rules. In §4, methods are grouped by their historical lineage, and the cross-cutting choices are called out explicitly.

What changed over time?

The main sequence is: exact probability correction → better-aligned and cheaper proposals → better use of verification slots → target-feature reuse → parallel drafting and overlapped scheduling. These are complementary changes. Distillation improves the overlap α; a tree improves the chance of finding a useful path for a given verification budget; diffusion reduces sequential draft passes; asynchronous execution reduces waiting. None of these alone removes target verification or guarantees a speedup at saturated load.

4Methods in depth

For each family, identify the proposal distribution, target work, distinctive trick, and failure mode.

4.0 Before the modern small-LM recipe

Blockwise Parallel Decoding (Stern et al., 2018) trained parallel predictors for several future positions, then kept the longest prefix validated by a scoring model. It established the draft–verify pattern for greedy sequence generation before today’s LLM serving setting. Its exact greedy mode and its more permissive quality/speed modes should be distinguished. [17]

SpecDec (Xia et al., 2023) trained a specialized non-autoregressive drafter for sequence-to-sequence tasks and used a verification method tuned for fast, high-quality generation. Its reported roughly 5× speedup was relative to the paper’s seq2seq/beam-search setting with comparable task quality; it is not a claim of exact sampling from an unchanged target. Staged Speculative Decoding then combined a token tree with a second speculation stage that accelerates the drafter itself, reporting 3.16× single-batch latency on its 762M GPT-2-L test. These works motivate two later themes: reduce the draft’s critical path and spend target verification on likely paths. [18] [19]

The first bottleneck: prediction can be parallel even when commitment is sequential

For a confirmed prefix x1:tx_{1:t}x1:t​, train predictor gjg_jgj​ to guess token xt+jx_{t+j}xt+j​ for offsets j=1,…,Kj=1,\ldots ,Kj=1,…,K. All predictors read a common representation; unlike an autoregressive draft, predictor 3 does not wait for the sampled output of predictor 2. Teacher-forced target evaluation can then score the whole guessed block in parallel, because all candidate token IDs are already known. The causality constraint applies to which prefix the model sees, not to whether those known positions can be evaluated by one batched matrix operation. [17]

The difficulty is that independent future-position predictions are marginal guesses under an uncertain future. “The cat” and “the dog” may each be plausible, while combining a noun from one continuation with the verb of another can produce an implausible sequence. This dependence gap explains why later methods add a tree of combinations, condition heads on previous guesses, or draft from target features. Relaxing the validation threshold can accept more tokens but changes the correctness contract. The lasting contribution is therefore the separation of parallel proposal from sequentially valid commitment, rather than any particular modern LLM speed number.

4.1 Independent small-model drafting

Leviathan et al. and Chen et al. pair a slow target with a much cheaper autoregressive LM. The drafter samples KKK tokens and retains each qiq_{i}qi​ needed for correction. The target evaluates the complete draft once. Verification uses the rule in §1. Chen et al. independently developed speculative sampling and reported about 2–2.5× acceleration for a 70B Chinchilla model in their distributed setup; Leviathan et al. reported roughly 2–3× for T5-XXL in theirs. These are author-specific setups, not a universal expected speedup. [1] [2]

The draft model must use the same token sequence space for straightforward tokenwise verification. A related checkpoint often works well because its tokenizer and distribution are similar. A smaller model is cheaper but may disagree more often; a larger draft can improve acceptance while consuming the saved latency. The right draft is the one that maximizes committed tokens per unit of draft plus verifier time, not simply the one with the highest next-token accuracy. Distillation on the target’s likely prompts may improve alignment, but its benefit should be measured on held-out workloads.

Variants that change the drafter or the stopping rule

DistillSpec trains the small model to overlap the target rather than merely imitate next-token labels. Its distinguishing choices are on-policy trajectories from the draft and a divergence selected for the decoding setting; these choices target accepted-prefix length under the draft’s actual rollout distribution. The authors report 10–45% improvement over standard speculative decoding on their evaluated tasks. Online Speculative Decoding keeps adapting drafts on recent user-query distributions, addressing deployment drift; the cost is continuing training and an operational feedback loop. Both still require target-side verification for exact generation. [21] [22]

SpecDec++ treats draft length as a stopping decision. A trained head estimates conditional acceptance; drafting ends when the predicted chance of a rejection passes a threshold derived from its cost model. It attacks wasted late draft steps on difficult contexts, whereas a fixed KKK assumes all contexts are alike. Ouroboros attacks serial draft latency differently: it extends drafts with candidate phrases retrieved from text generated during the current process, then verifies them. It is a hybrid of a neural drafter and phrase reuse rather than a new acceptance theorem. [23] [24]

A subtle deployment trap

A draft that is 20× smaller in parameter count need not be 20× faster for a single token. Kernel launches, low utilization, cross-device transfers, and separate KV-cache access can dominate. Test TdraftT_{\mathrm{draft}}Tdraft​ and acceptance together.

Draft training: cross-entropy, overlap, and the distribution of visited prefixes

Training a draft to minimize KL⁡(p∥q)\operatorname{KL}(p\|q)KL(p∥q) increases its likelihood on target-generated tokens. A useful theoretical bridge is Pinsker’s inequality: TV⁡(p,q)≤DKL(p∥q)/2\operatorname{TV}(p,q)\le\sqrt{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)/2}TV(p,q)≤DKL​(p∥q)/2​, so smaller forward KL can provide a lower bound on one-step acceptance. It does not directly minimize latency. Two equally sized drafts can have similar held-out cross-entropy and different acceptance along deployed prompts; two unequal drafts can trade higher acceptance for a much larger critical path. DistillSpec accordingly studies the data-generation distribution and distillation divergence, while Online Speculative Decoding updates the drafter on the requests actually encountered. [21] [22]

The distinction between teacher-forced prefixes and draft rollouts is crucial. A draft trained only on clean target contexts is deployed on its own unverified continuations. Those contexts can be off distribution, and an early error degrades every later guess. Training on target-sampled trajectories aligns with the served task; rollout-aware training exposes the head to its own errors. Neither change authorizes committing an unverified guess. Target verification is what permits aggressive approximation during training and proposal.

EK=1+∑i=1KPr⁡(Ai)CK=Tdraft+Tverify+Truntime(measured)EK+Pr⁡(AK+1)CK+ΔC>EKCK⟺Pr⁡(AK+1)ΔC>EKCK(ΔC>0)\begin{aligned}E_K&=1+\sum_{i=1}^K\Pr(A_i)\\ C_K&=T_{\mathrm{draft}}+T_{\mathrm{verify}}+T_{\mathrm{runtime}}\quad\text{(measured)}\\ \frac{E_K+\Pr(A_{K+1})}{C_K+\Delta C}&>\frac{E_K}{C_K}\\ \Longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{\Pr(A_{K+1})}{\Delta C}&>\frac{E_K}{C_K}\quad(\Delta C>0)\end{aligned}EK​CK​CK​+ΔCEK​+Pr(AK+1​)​⟺ΔCPr(AK+1​)​​=1+i=1∑K​Pr(Ai​)=Tdraft​+Tverify​+Truntime​(measured)>CK​EK​​>CK​EK​​(ΔC>0)​

This marginal test is a derivation from the speed objective, not a claim that the unknown future acceptance is directly observable. It says that the next speculation slot must earn more expected tokens per added millisecond than the current round. SpecDec++ and confidence-based early stopping estimate quantities related to that decision. Fixed draft lengths are reasonable when kernels require fixed shapes or profiling noise makes adaptation expensive; they are a hardware choice as well as an algorithm choice. [23]

2023 February — BiLD: adaptive collaboration and its exactness boundary

Big Little Decoder lets a small model continue while it is confident, falls back to the large model when confidence drops, and lets the large model roll back earlier small-model decisions judged inaccurate. Thus draft length emerges from the input instead of remaining fixed. It uses confidence/discrepancy policies rather than the canonical probability-ratio accept/reject rule. Its reported maximum 2.12× acceleration on NVIDIA T4 covered translation and summarization with small task-quality changes. Kim et al., 15 February 2023; NeurIPS 2023.

Why a confidence threshold alone cannot prove exactness

Suppose the small model assigns a token probability 0.99, while the target assigns it 0.70. Accepting it solely because 0.99 exceeds a threshold transfers excessive probability mass to that token. Under exact speculative sampling the acceptance probability would instead be 0.70/0.99. A rollback distance or a high benchmark score does not replace this accounting. BiLD is an important adaptive-decoding ancestor; its ordinary threshold policy should not be grouped with proven distribution-preserving samplers.

2023 October — Online Speculative Decoding and DistillSpec: train for acceptance

Online Speculative Decoding adapts one or several draft models to observed request traffic using verification feedback and online distillation. Its problem is distribution shift: a generally competent drafter can disagree systematically with the target on the service's actual requests. The paper reports acceptance-rate increases of 0.1–0.65 and 1.42–2.17× latency reductions in its evaluated settings. Feedback is available from target verification, but optimization, gradient memory, and model deployment still consume resources. Liu et al., 11 October 2023.

DistillSpec studies offline alignment more systematically: generate training contexts on-policy from the draft and select a divergence suited to the task and decoding regime. It reports 10–45% additional speedup over ordinary speculative decoding. Its separate lossy and target-distillation configurations must not be conflated with accelerating an unchanged target losslessly. Zhou et al., 12 October 2023.

Derivation: language-model quality and speculative utility differ
α(h)=∑vmin⁡[p(v∣h),qθ(v∣h)]=1−TV⁡(p(⋅∣h),qθ(⋅∣h))Ldistill(θ)=Eh∼Ddeployment or DdraftD(p(⋅∣h),qθ(⋅∣h))TV⁡(p,q)≤DKL(p∥q)2\begin{aligned}\alpha(h)&=\sum_v\min[p(v\mid h),q_\theta(v\mid h)]\\ &=1-\operatorname{TV}(p(\cdot\mid h),q_\theta(\cdot\mid h))\\ \mathcal L_{\mathrm{distill}}(\theta)&=\mathbb E_{h\sim\mathcal D_{\mathrm{deployment}}\text{ or }\mathcal D_{\mathrm{draft}}}D(p(\cdot\mid h),q_\theta(\cdot\mid h))\\ \operatorname{TV}(p,q)&\le\sqrt{\frac{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)}2}\end{aligned}α(h)Ldistill​(θ)TV(p,q)​=v∑​min[p(v∣h),qθ​(v∣h)]=1−TV(p(⋅∣h),qθ​(⋅∣h))=Eh∼Ddeployment​ or Ddraft​​D(p(⋅∣h),qθ​(⋅∣h))≤2DKL​(p∥q)​​​

The acceptance objective depends on overlap with this target, not agreement with a dataset's single reference answer. The KL bound explains one reason distillation can help, but it is only a bound: smaller average KL need not deliver the fastest drafter or the longest accepted prefix. Context sampling changes which disagreements receive weight. Online adaptation targets the deployment distribution; on-policy sampling exposes contexts the drafter actually visits. For exact sampling, each proposal must be verified using the proposal probabilities that generated it. Updating parameters mid-block and recomputing old probabilities with the new model breaks that contract.

2023 December — Cascade Speculative Drafting: speculate on the drafter

Vertical cascading recursively accelerates a neural drafter with a cheaper model, terminating in a statistical n-gram model. Horizontal cascading uses stronger drafting for early positions and cheaper drafting for later ones, whose survival probability is lower. These are distinct axes. The paper reports up to 81% additional speedup over its standard-speculation baseline; this is not 81% less latency or a universal 1.81× gain. Chen et al., first submitted 18 December 2023; revised method and experiments.

Why the suffix has lower economic value
sj=Pr⁡(first j proposals survive)=∏i=1jαiE=1+∑j=1Ksj∂E∂αj=∑k=jK∏1≤i≤ki≠jαi\begin{aligned}s_j&=\Pr(\text{first }j\text{ proposals survive})=\prod_{i=1}^j\alpha_i\\ E&=1+\sum_{j=1}^Ks_j\\ \frac{\partial E}{\partial\alpha_j}&=\sum_{k=j}^K\prod_{\substack{1\le i\le k\\i\ne j}}\alpha_i\end{aligned}sj​E∂αj​∂E​​=Pr(first j proposals survive)=i=1∏j​αi​=1+j=1∑K​sj​=k=j∑K​1≤i≤ki=j​∏​αi​​

Here αᵢ denotes acceptance conditional on surviving earlier positions. Improving an early decision benefits many later positions. A late expensive proposal may almost never be reached. This mathematical asymmetry motivates horizontal resource allocation; actual deployment must also include batch-dependent verifier cost and the extra caches of multiple models. In a vertical cascade, exact inner verification produces samples from the intermediate model; exact outer verification then produces samples from the target. Composition preserves the final distribution when every stage uses its actual conditional proposal law.

4.2 SpecInfer and tree verification

SpecInfer collects proposed continuations from one or several small models in a token tree. Shared prefixes are represented once; alternative branches cover different possible next tokens. A tree-aware causal attention mask ensures a node sees only its ancestors, so the target can score many branch contexts in one verification pass. The algorithm then selects a valid target-consistent path, with separate procedures for deterministic and stochastic decoding. Its paper reports 1.5–2.8× against prior distributed-serving systems and 2.6–3.5× in an offloading setting—situations where expensive target access makes wider verification attractive. [7]

A tree trades verifier work for acceptance coverage. Dense branching can be wasteful: when many siblings are scored but only one path survives, the added positions increase arithmetic and KV traffic. Tree construction, prefix deduplication, position IDs, attention masks, and committing only chosen-path cache entries are central systems problems. This idea later appears in Medusa and EAGLE, though their proposal models differ.

What later tree papers optimized

VariantDistinctive mechanismWhen it matters
Staged SD (2023)Speculate for the draft model too; combine stages with a tree.Draft-model latency itself is significant. [19]
Sequoia (2024)Dynamic program chooses a tree under a node budget and a positional acceptance model; its verification samples draft alternatives without replacement and tunes size/depth to hardware.Large budgets, varying temperatures, expensive target access. [25]
SpecExec (2024)Builds a high-probability draft “cache” tree for target verification.Consumer GPUs offloading large target weights to RAM. [26]
OPT-Tree (2024/25)Greedily grows a context-dependent tree to maximize estimated accepted length under a node limit.Draft confidence varies with the current prompt. [27]
DySpec (2024)Dynamically expands branches using draft-probability estimates correlated with acceptance.Fixed topology wastes nodes on easy or hard contexts. [28]
Multi-draft sampling (2024)Uses several independent proposals and an exact token-selection coupling; accepting “any matching one” naively is not exact.Proposal diversity is worth extra draft/verify work. [29]

Important distinction: Sequoia’s tree optimizer relies on a position-of-child acceptance approximation, while OPT-Tree and DySpec adapt the shape to the current draft probabilities. EAGLE-2 applies a similar context-dependent idea to EAGLE’s target-aware drafter. None of these tree-selection heuristics replaces the final target verification. [8] [25] [27] [28]

A newer branch, DARTree (2026), uses a diffusion-style parallel tree drafter while preserving autoregressive dependencies along candidate paths. Its paper reports up to 12.97 accepted tokens per verification round and 9.73× in selected within-paper tests. The proposal geometry attacks both sequential drafting and independent-position inconsistency. Treat its August 2026 preprint comparisons as promising evidence to reproduce under your own target and runtime. [48]

Tree attention is an execution transformation; tree sampling is a probability algorithm

Flatten a candidate tree into nodes v=1,…,Nv=1,\ldots ,Nv=1,…,N. For each node retain its token ID, parent index, depth, and proposal information. Assign a position ID from depth, so siblings at the same depth share the appropriate autoregressive position; flattening order is a storage address, not the token’s logical position. An attention mask allows the permanent prefix plus ancestors on the node’s unique root-to-node path. With that mask, the target hidden state at a node equals the state for the corresponding standalone path, up to numerical implementation differences. [7]

After selecting an accepted path, gather only its KV entries into permanent sequence order. Unselected sibling KV must not survive. Distinguish the logit produced at a node, which predicts its children, from the probability used to accept the node itself, which comes from its parent. Confusing those two offsets produces a plausible-looking but incorrect verifier. A tree may have dozens of nodes but commit only one path, so expected progress is governed by coverage of probable paths rather than the total number of evaluated tokens.

Masking alone does not prove stochastic exactness. A top-k tree, candidates drawn without replacement, and independent samples from a draft have different proposal laws. SpecInfer couples its tree representation with a tree-based verification procedure. One cannot take an arbitrary tree builder and accept every sibling using min⁡ ⁣(1,pq)\min\!\left(1,\frac pq\right)min(1,qp​) against the original unmodified distributions: a rejected sibling changes the residual mass available to later alternatives. The probability algorithm must account for that sequence of events.

Multiple proposals: the object being coupled is now a set or tuple

Keep this guide’s notation p=target, q=draftp=\mathrm{target},\ q=\mathrm{draft}p=target, q=draft; some papers reverse those letters. Suppose S=(X1,…,Xk)S=(X_{1},\ldots ,X_{k})S=(X1​,…,Xk​) is an ordered tuple of proposals with joint law QQQ. SpecTr asks for a coupling π(S,y)\pi (S,y)π(S,y) with tuple marginal Q(S)Q(S)Q(S) and output marginal p(y)p(y)p(y) that maximizes the chance that yyy is already in the tuple. A transport formulation makes the constraints explicit: [49]

maximize⁡π∑S∑yπ(S,y)1y∈Ssubject to∑yπ(S,y)=Q(S)∑Sπ(S,y)=p(y),π(S,y)≥0\begin{aligned}\underset{\pi}{\operatorname{maximize}}\quad&\sum_S\sum_y\pi(S,y)\mathbf1_{y\in S}\\ \text{subject to}\quad&\sum_y\pi(S,y)=Q(S)\\ &\sum_S\pi(S,y)=p(y),\quad\pi(S,y)\ge0\end{aligned}πmaximize​subject to​S∑​y∑​π(S,y)1y∈S​y∑​π(S,y)=Q(S)S∑​π(S,y)=p(y),π(S,y)≥0​

The vocabulary and tuple space make the literal linear program too large to solve online. SpecTr develops an efficient valid transport construction with a stated 1−1e1-\frac1e1−e1​ approximation guarantee for its optimal-acceptance objective. This is a guarantee about the construction’s objective under its assumptions, not a bound on end-to-end GPU speedup. Target evaluation cost, candidate multiplicity, and sampling work still determine performance.

A useful impossibility example requires no solver. If q(A)=0.2q(A)=0.2q(A)=0.2 and there are two independent drafts, the probability that either contains AAA is 1−0.82=0.361-0.8^{2}=0.361−0.82=0.36. If p(A)=0.8p(A)=0.8p(A)=0.8, an algorithm that always outputs a proposed token cannot produce the required 0.8 mass on AAA. At least 0.44 of total output probability must come from outcomes where a correction supplies AAA. More generally, always accepting a candidate requires p(U)≤Pr⁡(S∩U≠∅)p(U)\le\Pr(S\cap U\ne\varnothing)p(U)≤Pr(S∩U=∅) for every vocabulary subset UUU. For independent drafts the right side is 1−(1−q(U))k1-(1-q(U))^k1−(1−q(U))k. This is a necessary coverage constraint, not merely a top-1 accuracy criterion.

The canonical multi-draft framework organizes this into two stages. First select an intermediate candidate using conditional weights βy(S)\beta _y(S)βy​(S), giving induced token law m(y)=∑SQ(S)βy(S)m(y)=\sum_SQ(S)\beta_y(S)m(y)=∑S​Q(S)βy​(S). Then perform maximal coupling between mmm and ppp, correcting any unmatched residual. The acceptance objective becomes ∑ymin⁡(m(y),p(y))\sum_y\min(m(y),p(y))∑y​min(m(y),p(y)). The subtlety is that the relevant proposal distribution is mmm, not the original per-draft qqq. Selecting the highest-scoring candidate changes its law. This perspective helps classify multi-draft algorithms by where their selection or correction approximations enter. [29]

Sequoia’s dynamic program: make the assumption visible

Under Sequoia’s positional acceptance model, let aja_jaj​ be the conditional probability of selecting the j-th child, given that its parent has been reached. These are verification/acceptance probabilities, not raw softmax values. The probability of reaching node vvv is the product of the relevant child probabilities along its path. Expected accepted length is therefore a sum of reach probabilities. Define F(n,b)F(n,b)F(n,b) as the maximum expected visited-node count for a rooted n-node tree with b children at the root; include the root as one unit. The recurrence allocates m nodes to the last child’s subtree: [25]

F(1,0)=1F(n,b)=max⁡1≤m≤n−1[F(n−m,b−1)+abmax⁡jF(m,j)]Node contribution=∏edges on its pathPr⁡(child accepted)\begin{aligned}F(1,0)&=1\\ F(n,b)&=\max_{1\le m\le n-1}\left[F(n-m,b-1)+a_b\max_jF(m,j)\right]\\ \text{Node contribution}&=\prod_{\text{edges on its path}}\Pr(\text{child accepted})\end{aligned}F(1,0)F(n,b)Node contribution​=1=1≤m≤n−1max​[F(n−m,b−1)+ab​jmax​F(m,j)]=edges on its path∏​Pr(child accepted)​

Only feasible states participate in the maximum. Add a depth bound when draft latency grows with the number of sequential expansion steps. Profile target verification for different node counts and choose the tree whose predicted expected progress divided by measured cost is highest. The recurrence is optimal inside the assumed acceptance model; context-dependent confidence, prefix-dependent acceptance, and a different verifier can invalidate a fixed aja_jaj​ estimate. EAGLE-2’s dynamic confidence tree and Sequoia’s budget optimization address related allocation problems with different information and cost assumptions. The useful design pattern is to separate probability model, tree optimizer, and hardware cost model, then test each separately.

Derivation: why an ancestor mask reproduces serial target states

Consider a causal transformer with tokenwise normalization and MLPs, the same target weights, and deterministic evaluation. A candidate tree contains token-labelled nodes; a node v at depth d represents the unique candidate path from the root to v. The confirmed prefix has n tokens at positions 0 through n−1. Assign v position n+d−1, regardless of its location in a flattened batch.

For v, allow attention to every confirmed-prefix key and to candidate keys on v's ancestor path including v itself. Exclude siblings and their descendants. If qᵥ,kᵤ are the query/key vectors at one layer, this masked attention is:

Avu=softmax⁡u ⁣(qv⊤kudh+Mvu)Mvu={0,u in confirmed prefix or path(root→v)−∞,otherwise\begin{aligned}A_{vu}&=\operatorname{softmax}_u\!\left(\frac{q_v^\top k_u}{\sqrt{d_h}}+M_{vu}\right)\\ M_{vu}&=\begin{cases}0,&u\text{ in confirmed prefix or path(root}\to v\text{)}\\-\infty,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\end{aligned}Avu​Mvu​​=softmaxu​(dh​​qv⊤​ku​​+Mvu​)={0,−∞,​u in confirmed prefix or path(root→v)otherwise​​

Prove equality to a separate serial target run on that path by induction on layers. At layer zero, v has the same token embedding and position, and each visible predecessor does too. If layer-ℓ states match, projected Q/K/V and all visible logits match. The mask exposes exactly the serial predecessor set, so the softmax denominator and weighted value sum match. Tokenwise residual, normalization and MLP operations preserve equality. Therefore final logits at v predict the distribution for a child after v's entire path.

There are two indexing details. A candidate's probability is read from its parent's logits, not from logits after the candidate itself. The first candidate uses the confirmed prefix's next-token logits. Also, equal-depth siblings share position IDs but are not the same cache entry; their hidden states depend on different tokens. Flattened array indices must never silently become semantic positions.

This is an equivalence proof in exact arithmetic under these architectural assumptions. Token-batch-dependent capacity dropping in a MoE, noncausal cross-token modules, altered positional rules, or changed floating-point reductions require separate analysis. After branch selection, only KV entries on the committed path survive; logits from discarded siblings are not valid continuation states.

Exercise — Find the sibling contamination

The confirmed prefix ends at P. Candidate children are A and B; A has child C. Which candidate nodes may C attend to? Which logits score the probability of C? What changes if C attends to B as well?

Show worked solution

C may attend to A and C itself, plus the confirmed prefix; it must not attend to sibling branch B. The logits after A score C. Allowing B introduces an extra key/value into C’s softmax denominator and value sum, so C’s hidden state no longer equals the target run on P,A,C. Even if C was accepted using the correct parent logits, the contaminated state could corrupt its later children and bonus token.

Derivation: multiple proposals change the probability law after selection

A tree can raise the probability that a desired token is present, but coverage is not itself a sampling rule. To isolate the issue, draw m independent candidates from a Bernoulli proposal q with q(A)=u. A deterministic selector returns A if any candidate is A, otherwise B. The selected token has distribution s, obtained by summing over candidate sets:

s(B)=Pr⁡(all m candidates are B)=(1−u)ms(A)=1−(1−u)m\begin{aligned}s(B)&=\Pr(\text{all }m\text{ candidates are }B)=(1-u)^m\\ s(A)&=1-(1-u)^m\end{aligned}s(B)s(A)​=Pr(all m candidates are B)=(1−u)m=1−(1−u)m​

If this selected token is then used as a single proposal, exact rejection correction must use s, not q: accept x with min(1,p(x)/s(x)) and draw rejected mass from (p−s)₊. More general tree verifiers can couple directly to the candidate set and use a different valid algorithm; the point is that the probability law of selection is part of the proof.

For any single-token coupling whose two marginals are s and p, diagonal mass at x cannot exceed either s(x) or p(x), hence cannot exceed min(s(x),p(x)). Summing gives a maximum equality probability Σx min(s(x),p(x))=1−TV(s,p). The ordinary rejection construction attains this bound. This optimality is for the specified one-token marginals; it does not prove an arbitrary tree algorithm is optimal in latency or accepted path length.

A set can contain many useful candidates while selection concentrates excessively on one token. Conversely, selecting a candidate close to the target can improve overlap but increase target or draft compute. Tree width, selection law, verifier semantics and cost must be evaluated together.

Exercise — Quantify the bias from using the original proposal probability

Let p(A)=0.5, q(A)=0.4 and m=2. Select A whenever it appears among the two proposals. Compute s. Then compare correct rejection against s with an incorrect rejection rule using q and residual (p−q)₊.

Show worked solution

s(A)=1−0.6²=0.64 and s(B)=0.36. Correct acceptance probabilities are 0.5/0.64=0.78125 for A and 1 for B. Accepted mass is (0.5,0.36), and rejected mass 0.14 is assigned to B; final law is (0.5,0.5).

The incorrect q-based rule always accepts selected A, since 0.5/0.4>1, and accepts B with probability 0.5/0.6=5/6. Its accepted mass is (0.64,0.30); the remaining 0.06 is sent to A by (p−q)₊. The final distribution is (0.70,0.30), far from p. Correcting a transformed proposal with its pre-selection probabilities is the error.

4.3 Medusa, Hydra, and model-native MTP

Medusa adds lightweight decoding heads to a target’s hidden state. Head jjj predicts the token jjj positions ahead; top candidates from the heads form a sparse tree. One target pass with tree attention verifies it. Medusa-1 freezes the original backbone and trains heads. Medusa-2 jointly tunes the backbone and heads, improving draft quality but changing the reference model itself. The paper reports 2.18× for Medusa-1 and 2.83× for Medusa-2 on its Vicuna-7B setup against its stated baseline. The rejection-sampling option preserves the reference target distribution; the paper’s “typical acceptance” intentionally trades exactness for more accepted candidates and similar measured quality. [3]

Hydra addresses a weakness of independent future-token heads: head jjj should know what earlier heads proposed. Its heads condition sequentially on prior draft tokens, so later guesses can respond to the actual candidate prefix. This adds cheap serial work but improves coherent multi-token predictions. The Hydra++ paper reports up to 1.31× throughput over its Medusa configuration and 2.70× over autoregressive decoding in its evaluation. Preserve the chosen verifier’s rule when interpreting exactness; better heads alone do not guarantee it. [4]

Multi-token prediction (MTP) makes future-token prediction part of the model’s training or architecture. DeepSeek-V3, for example, describes sequential MTP modules that retain a causal chain across prediction depths. Its report gives an 85–90% second-token acceptance rate across its tested topics and 1.8× decoding tokens/s with this feature. An MTP module is a proposer, not a replacement for target verification. Whether the served configuration is exact depends on its acceptance logic and which model distribution is defined as the target. Native MTP avoids a separately loaded draft checkpoint but couples the optimization to the model family. [5]

ReDrafter replaces a collection of independent future heads with a small recurrent drafter conditioned on target hidden states. It uses beam search for several sequences, then packs their shared prefixes into a dynamic tree to avoid sending duplicates to the verifier. The original paper reports up to 2.8× on H100 MT-Bench and 2.3× on Apple Silicon in its respective implementations. Its beam width must be tuned to device capacity: wider beams improve coverage but increase verification cost. [30]

Speculative Streaming goes further into the target architecture. It fine-tunes a single model with future nnn-gram prediction and speculative streams, aiming to draft and verify in one model without auxiliary draft weights. This is a changed model and should be evaluated against the corresponding fine-tuned baseline. Its paper reports 1.8–3.1× across its selected tasks with comparable generation quality; it does not establish identity to an untouched pretrained checkpoint. [31]

Why heads save work, and where they lose dependency information

Let hth_tht​ be the target’s last hidden state. A Medusa head can be written schematically as qj=softmax⁡(WjMLP⁡j(ht))q_j=\operatorname{softmax}(W_j\operatorname{MLP}_j(h_t))qj​=softmax(Wj​MLPj​(ht​)), predicting a future offset j with an auxiliary cross-entropy loss. One expensive backbone traversal supplies every head’s input. However, q2(xt+2∣ht)q_{2}(x_{t+2}\mid h_t)q2​(xt+2​∣ht​) is not the same conditional as q2(xt+2∣ht,xt+1)q_{2}(x_{t+2}\mid h_t,x_{t+1})q2​(xt+2​∣ht​,xt+1​). A high-confidence second-position token can belong to a different continuation than the selected first-position token. Enumerating k candidates at each of d offsets creates up to kdk^{d}kd paths; a sparse, calibrated tree spends verification slots on combinations that often succeed. [3]

Read Medusa’s acceptance options carefully. Typical acceptance compares a token’s target likelihood against a threshold related to the target entropy, admitting plausible alternatives even if they are not the greedy answer. That can improve speed while maintaining measured quality, but it is not the residual construction’s exact distribution guarantee. Medusa-1 freezes the original backbone when training heads. Medusa-2 jointly trains the backbone and heads, so exact verification, if used, preserves the resulting fine-tuned checkpoint. A comparison with the pre-fine-tuning model then has two moving parts: the sampler and the model distribution.

Hydra changes the factorization: q(xt+1:t+K∣ht)=∏jqj(xt+j∣ht,xt+1:t+j−1)q(x_{t+1:t+K}\mid h_t)=\prod_jq_j(x_{t+j}\mid h_t,x_{t+1:t+j-1})q(xt+1:t+K​∣ht​)=∏j​qj​(xt+j​∣ht​,xt+1:t+j−1​). Lightweight heads consume embeddings of the speculative prefix, making their future guesses coherent with earlier choices. This introduces a dependency chain among small heads, but the chain is much cheaper than K complete target traversals. Its value depends on whether improved acceptance outweighs this extra proposal work. The contrast with Medusa is instructive: improving each independent marginal is not the only route to better drafting; changing which variables the predictor conditions on can be more important. [4]

Model-native multi-token prediction, such as DeepSeek-V3’s auxiliary MTP modules, occupies a related design space. Shared representations and offset supervision make extra predictions inexpensive, while sequentially connected modules recover some cross-token dependence. MTP can be a training regularizer, an inference drafter, or both. An MTP training loss by itself says nothing about whether a particular serving implementation verifies the proposed tokens exactly. [5]

2024 April → December — MTP moves drafting into pretraining

Meta's multi-token prediction trains several future-token heads over a shared trunk. It is simultaneously a representation-learning objective and a way to provide speculative candidates. Its 4-token models obtain up to 3× inference acceleration in the paper, while the 13B experiments also show coding-quality improvements. These are separate claims: improved training does not itself prove exact inference. Gloeckle et al., 30 April 2024.

LMeta-MTP=−∑t∑k=1Klog⁡pk(xt+k∣ht)ht=shared trunk⁡(x≤t)\begin{aligned}\mathcal L_{\mathrm{Meta\text{-}MTP}}&=-\sum_t\sum_{k=1}^K\log p_k(x_{t+k}\mid h_t)\\ h_t&=\operatorname{shared\ trunk}(x_{\le t})\end{aligned}LMeta-MTP​ht​​=−t∑​k=1∑K​logpk​(xt+k​∣ht​)=shared trunk(x≤t​)​

Heads can propose simultaneously, but predictions from a shared prefix omit the dependencies induced by the sampled intermediate tokens. The main next-token branch must still verify them. Auxiliary heads can be discarded for ordinary decoding; retaining them trades added inference work for fewer large-model iterations.

DeepSeek-V3 MTP instead chains prediction modules, preserving a causal chain through earlier predicted features and shifted token embeddings. Each module merges a normalized previous-depth representation with a normalized next-token embedding, projects them, and applies a Transformer block. Embedding and output components are shared. DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report, December 2024, §2.2 and §5.4.3.

ztk=Mk[RMSNorm⁡(htk−1);RMSNorm⁡(Emb⁡(xt+k))]htk=Transformer⁡k(z≤tk)ptk=SharedOutput⁡(htk)predicting xt+k+1\begin{aligned}z_t^k&=M_k[\operatorname{RMSNorm}(h_t^{k-1});\operatorname{RMSNorm}(\operatorname{Emb}(x_{t+k}))]\\ h_t^k&=\operatorname{Transformer}_k(z_{\le t}^k)\\ p_t^k&=\operatorname{SharedOutput}(h_t^k)\quad\text{predicting }x_{t+k+1}\end{aligned}ztk​htk​ptk​​=Mk​[RMSNorm(htk−1​);RMSNorm(Emb(xt+k​))]=Transformerk​(z≤tk​)=SharedOutput(htk​)predicting xt+k+1​​

Training uses the observed shifted tokens; inference supplies generated proposals. V3 reports 85–90% acceptance for the second-token prediction and 1.8× tokens/s using its MTP module. That is a shallow production-oriented configuration, not evidence that arbitrarily long MTP chains retain the same acceptance. The chain improves conditional information but reintroduces serial draft work. This tension directly motivates later hybrid parallel/sequential drafters.

Exercise: is the better drafter faster?

Target time is 10 ms, verification of four candidates costs 12 ms, and both systems use K = 4. Drafter A costs 1 ms per token with conditional acceptance α = 0.8; B costs 2 ms with α = 0.9. Ignore other overhead. Compute speedups and decide.

Show derivation and answer
EA=1+0.8+0.82+0.83+0.84=3.3616SA=10⋅3.361612+4⋅1=2.101EB=1+0.9+0.92+0.93+0.94=4.0951SB=10⋅4.095112+4⋅2=2.048\begin{aligned}E_A&=1+0.8+0.8^2+0.8^3+0.8^4=3.3616\\ S_A&=\frac{10\cdot3.3616}{12+4\cdot1}=2.101\\ E_B&=1+0.9+0.9^2+0.9^3+0.9^4=4.0951\\ S_B&=\frac{10\cdot4.0951}{12+4\cdot2}=2.048\end{aligned}EA​SA​EB​SB​​=1+0.8+0.82+0.83+0.84=3.3616=12+4⋅110⋅3.3616​=2.101=1+0.9+0.92+0.93+0.94=4.0951=12+4⋅210⋅4.0951​=2.048​

A wins despite lower acceptance. Improving overlap only helps if the increase in committed tokens exceeds the relative increase in iteration time. The calculation assumes homogeneous conditional acceptance and fixed verifier latency; measured values should replace these assumptions in a serving system.

4.4 EAGLE, EAGLE-2, EAGLE-3

EAGLE uses a lightweight autoregressive drafter conditioned on target-model information. Instead of learning only future token logits from scratch, the original EAGLE predicts a second-to-top-layer target feature and uses the target LM head to turn that feature into a draft-token distribution. It also conditions on the sampled next token to reduce feature uncertainty: multiple plausible tokens can correspond to ambiguous future features. The target still verifies proposed tokens. In the paper’s Llama2-chat-70B experiments, reported latency speedup is about 2.7–3.5×. [6]

EAGLE-2 changes the candidate selection strategy. A fixed tree spends the same branch budget regardless of whether the current prefix is easy or uncertain. EAGLE-2 uses draft confidence as an approximation to acceptance probability, expands promising branches, and dynamically forms a context-dependent tree for target verification. Its paper reports 3.05–4.26× across its evaluated model/task combinations and says the output distribution remains unchanged under its verifier. The gain is a joint effect of a good EAGLE draft, tree allocation, and the execution system. [8]

EAGLE-3 revises the drafter again: it removes the requirement to regress a specific future target feature, directly trains token prediction, fuses target features from low, middle, and high layers, and uses a training-time procedure that exposes the drafter to its own multi-step predictions. It keeps the target verification principle and can use the EAGLE-2 tree strategy. Its paper reports up to 6.5× in selected latency experiments and 1.38× throughput at batch size 64 in SGLang. Those results are not entries in the older Spec-Bench table below and should not be ranked against it without matched workloads. [9]

The EAGLE progression

EAGLE: predict target-like features → sample candidate tokens. EAGLE-2: allocate a dynamic draft tree using confidence. EAGLE-3: train a direct-token, multi-layer-feature drafter with multi-step exposure. The target verifier remains the authority in all three.

HASS is a side branch from the EAGLE-style target-aware drafter: it studies the mismatch between training contexts/objectives and rollout-time contexts/objectives, then harmonizes both without extra inference overhead. Its paper reports 2.81–4.05× in its LLaMA experiments and 8–20% better speedup than EAGLE-2 in those comparisons. Falcon pursues semi-autoregressive drafting: it predicts a block with a compact two-layer drafter, explicitly models within-block dependence, and builds a customized tree. Its AAAI paper reports 2.91–3.51× lossless speedup on its Vicuna/LLaMA2-Chat configurations. These are different changes to the EAGLE bottleneck, not successive official EAGLE versions. [32] [33]

EAGLE-1: predict an easier representation, but condition on the missing random variable

After the target processes token xtx_txt​, it has feature ftf_tft​ and can sample xt+1x_{t+1}xt+1​. The next target feature depends on that actual sampled token. Predicting ft+1f_{t+1}ft+1​ only from ftf_tft​ would average over several possible futures. EAGLE feeds the shifted token embedding e(xt+1)e(x_{t+1})e(xt+1​) alongside the current feature into a small autoregressive predictor. The predicted feature passes through the target’s LM head to propose subsequent tokens. The target’s rich state supplies information that a tiny standalone LM would otherwise have to reconstruct. [6]

The training objective combines a feature regression term with a token-level term through the target LM head. Feature matching transfers target structure, but errors in autoregressively predicted features can accumulate. This is why training data, feature noise, rollout length, and the weighting of feature versus token loss affect acceptance. It also motivates a later question: does the draft need to reproduce the target’s exact high-dimensional feature, or only the information necessary to predict its tokens?

EAGLE-2: use scarce target positions on the current request’s likely paths

A static tree allocates the same branching pattern to a nearly deterministic code fragment and an ambiguous natural-language continuation. EAGLE-2 instead uses draft confidence to expand promising nodes and globally rank candidate paths. A typical score multiplies conditional draft probabilities along the path, or sums their logarithms. This favors a deeper continuation when its prefix is confident, but spends more width near an uncertain fork. After selecting nodes, the verifier still needs an ancestor-consistent tree, position IDs, and a mask constructed from parent relationships. [8]

Confidence is a surrogate for acceptance. Under stochastic maximal coupling, a token’s acceptance also depends on the target-to-draft ratio; a confidently wrong draft is not useful. EAGLE-2’s empirical correlation makes confidence useful for allocating work, while its verifier carries the fidelity guarantee. A practical diagnostic is to bin proposed nodes by confidence and measure target acceptance in each bin, separately by depth and task. A calibration failure harms efficiency even when every generated output remains correct.

EAGLE-3: remove unnecessary feature constraints and train the actual feedback loop

Construct a fused context feature gt=Wf[ftlow;ftmid;fthigh]g_t=W_f[f_t^{\mathrm{low}};f_t^{\mathrm{mid}};f_t^{\mathrm{high}}]gt​=Wf​[ftlow​;ftmid​;fthigh​]. Combine it with the shifted token embedding, project into the draft decoder’s input width, and produce draft state at+1a_{t+1}at+1​. The shared target LM head maps that state to token logits. At the first step, the real target features are available from prefill or verification. At later speculative steps, the target has not run yet, so the drafter feeds its own previous state back. Requiring that state to match one specific future target feature would constrain the draft’s representation more than token agreement requires. [9]

EAGLE-3 removes the feature prediction loss and explicitly trains multi-step feedback through its training-time test mechanism. The two changes complement each other: direct token training increases representational freedom; simulated inference exposes the model to its own states. HASS addresses related rollout/context and objective mismatches within the feature-drafting line. EAGLE-3 goes further by replacing the regression target itself and using features from several target layers. These are substantive algorithmic changes, so “EAGLE-3 is EAGLE-2 with a wider tree” misses the source of its improvement. [32] [9]

The three-version trajectory separates three research questions: what information should the drafter receive (EAGLE-1), where should verification work be allocated (EAGLE-2), and what internal state and training objective should the drafter use (EAGLE-3). Tree policy, feature fusion, and rollout training can be ablated independently. For a deployment, also count feature extraction/copy overhead, compatibility with tensor parallelism, draft KV storage, and the need to retrain heads after changing the target checkpoint.

Derivation: distribution matching and hidden-state matching optimize different quantities

At a fixed target prefix, let target probabilities p be fixed and qθ=softmax(zθ). Distillation cross-entropy is L=−Σx p(x)log qθ(x). Differentiate using ∂log q(x)/∂z(y)=1[x=y]−q(y):

∂L∂z(y)=−p(y)+q(y)∑xp(x)=q(y)−p(y)L=H(p)+DKL(p∥q)\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial z(y)}&=-p(y)+q(y)\sum_xp(x)=q(y)-p(y)\\ \mathcal L&=H(p)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\end{aligned}∂z(y)∂L​L​=−p(y)+q(y)x∑​p(x)=q(y)−p(y)=H(p)+DKL​(p∥q)​

Thus its optimum over unrestricted q is p. The exact one-step acceptance rate is α=Σx min(p(x),q(x))=1−½∥p−q∥₁. These objectives share their optimum but are not numerically identical away from it. Top-1 agreement discards still more information: p=(0.51,0.49) and q=(0.99,0.01) have the same argmax but acceptance only 0.51+0.01=0.52.

For a feature drafter, write a target output head z=Wh+b and a feature prediction ĥ=h+δ. The resulting logit perturbation is Wδ. First-order probability perturbation is J Wδ, where J=diag(p)−ppᵀ is the softmax Jacobian at the target logits. Therefore the local acceptance loss is approximately:

1−α≈12∥[diag⁡(p)−pp⊤]Wδ∥1\begin{aligned}1-\alpha&\approx\frac12\left\|[\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^\top]W\delta\right\|_1\end{aligned}1−α​≈21​​[diag(p)−pp⊤]Wδ​1​​

Feature MSE minimizes ∥δ∥² and treats all directions equally. Actual distribution error weights directions by W and the current softmax sensitivity. A feature error lying in the output head's nullspace has no direct logit effect; adding the same constant to all logits also changes no probabilities. A smaller Euclidean feature error is therefore not a universal guarantee of higher acceptance. The linearization is valid for sufficiently small perturbations and fixed output processing; top-k boundaries can break smoothness.

Finally, a teacher-forced loss averages over target-data prefixes, while a multi-step drafter encounters its own provisional prefixes and feature predictions. Future error can feed back into future proposals. This explains why training with rollout context, multiple future objectives, or target-token supervision can matter beyond reducing a one-step MSE. The formula is an explanatory local analysis, not a claim that every EAGLE variant optimizes this exact norm.

Exercise — A large feature error with no distribution error

Let W=[[1,0],[−1,0]], h=(0,0), and no bias. Compare δ₁=(0,10) with δ₂=(0.1,0). Which has larger feature error, and which changes target probabilities?

Show worked solution

δ₁ has norm 10, but Wδ₁=(0,0), so q remains (0.5,0.5) and acceptance is 1. δ₂ has norm 0.1, but logits become (0.1,−0.1), giving q(A)=1/(1+exp(−0.2))≈0.549834 and q(B)≈0.450166. Against p=(0.5,0.5), acceptance is 0.950166. Feature norm alone ranked these two errors in the wrong order for proposal acceptance.

4.5 Self speculative decoding: Draft & Verify and LayerSkip

Draft & Verify uses the target model itself as the draft by skipping selected intermediate Transformer layers during the proposal phase. A full-layer pass then verifies the guesses. It needs no separately trained draft model or extra draft weights; the paper reports up to 1.99× and describes identical final output to the unaltered model. Read this as a claim about the paper’s evaluated decoding procedure, rather than a blanket guarantee for every sampling configuration. A poor skip pattern harms acceptance; too little skipping makes the draft slow. [10]

LayerSkip trains the backbone to support early exits: later layers receive more layer dropout during training, and intermediate layers share an early-exit language-model loss. During inference, early layers draft while the remaining layers verify and correct, sharing activations and some computation. The benefit is better early predictions without a second full LM, at the price of a special training recipe and an implementation that retains reusable state correctly. The paper reports up to 2.16× on its summarization test, 1.82× on code, and 2.0× on semantic parsing. [11]

Kangaroo keeps a shallow target sub-network as its self-drafter and trains a small adapter to improve its predictions. Its “double early exit” means that it both exits the full model early to draft and ends a draft chain when the shallow model’s confidence becomes too low. On Spec-Bench it reports up to 1.68× with a single candidate chain; the 67M adapter is substantially smaller than the Medusa-1 head addition in its comparison. SWIFT removes even that adapter: it selects skipped intermediate layers on the fly for the current task or input stream, without new training. Its paper reports about 1.3–1.6× with target-distribution-preserving verification. These solve different problems: Kangaroo spends a little training to improve a very shallow draft; SWIFT tunes the skip pattern at deployment. [34] [35]

These methods are appealing when model memory is tight, but “self” does not mean free: omitted layers still have to be run for verification, and the same GPU executes both phases. Compare saved target invocations with extra layer execution and cache traffic. LayerSkip changes training; Draft & Verify and SWIFT can start from an existing checkpoint; Kangaroo adds adapter training.

Early-exit training and cache sharing are both necessary parts of the method

An ordinary transformer’s intermediate hidden states are not trained to be good final answers. LayerSkip makes them useful by applying more layer dropout at greater depth and sharing a language-model head across early exits. Schematically, the loss is ∑ℓwℓCE⁡(head⁡(norm⁡(hℓ)),xnext)\sum_\ell w_\ell\operatorname{CE}(\operatorname{head}(\operatorname{norm}(h_\ell)),x_{\mathrm{next}})∑ℓ​wℓ​CE(head(norm(hℓ​)),xnext​), with the paper’s layer sampling, schedules, and normalization controlling which exits receive supervision. Sharing the output head avoids a separate vocabulary-sized matrix for every exit, but the backbone must learn features that are interpretable before the final layer. [11]

At inference, choose exit depth e. The first e layers draft a chain and retain their KV plus the hidden vectors needed by layers e+1 through L.
